meta.title: Will AI Make Our Jobs Obsolete? Why I Decided to Prepare
meta.seoTitle: AI and Jobs: Preparing for the Future
meta.description: Why I worry about extensive automation of knowledge work, what the research says and how to think through a personal strategy for the years ahead.
meta.excerpt: The 80% figure is my hypothesis, not a statistic. Here is why I take this risk seriously and how I want to help people think about their future.
meta.coverAlt: Silhouette of a man standing by a window in a dark room.

content.text: We may be at the start of an economic and social upheaval far deeper than we imagine. I want to explain why I think the next ten years could change our relationship with work, and why I built a tool to help people think about their own future.

sections.title: A conviction that may sound extreme

content.text: I’ll start with a fairly radical claim: within five to ten years, artificial intelligence could make up to 80% of today’s knowledge work jobs done at a computer redundant.
That figure comes from no study. It’s my own intuition, and I can’t prove it today.

I’m a developer. I use these tools every day to build applications, and I can see how quickly they’re improving. The more I use them, the harder it is to imagine our workplaces carrying on as they are.

A few years ago, building an application took weeks or even months. Now some tasks that used to take me several days take a few minutes. That’s not true of everything: AI still makes mistakes, and a project’s complexity doesn’t magically disappear. But I find it hard to ignore the direction things are going.
And I see no reason for progress to stop where it is.

sections.title: The real shock will be economic

content.text: AI is often presented as a tool that will make us more productive. That’s true, but too often the discussion ends there.

Take a company with ten people providing a digital service. If AI means three people can do the same work tomorrow, the company has several options: produce more, cut prices, launch new services… or reduce headcount.
Some people think productivity gains will generate enough new activity to make up for the jobs lost. That’s possible. Innovation has often created jobs that no one saw coming.

This time, though, something feels different. AI is getting better at the very things that have helped us adapt in the past: learning, reasoning, creating and solving problems. It can already take over some tasks. If new jobs emerge, there’s no guarantee that they won’t be automated in turn.
Even if companies keep their staff, they can simply hire fewer people. Unemployment could grow through layoffs and through opportunities quietly disappearing.
We’re already seeing some signals. In August 2026,
Stanford researchers

updated their study of employment among Americans aged 22 to 25. In jobs with the highest AI exposure, employment among that group is about 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with employment in less exposed jobs. That’s a relative gap: it doesn’t mean that AI eliminated 19% of jobs. The researchers say they can’t tell how much of the gap is due to generative AI, and they don’t find widespread job losses across the economy. The gap does, however, seem to come mainly from fewer hires, which echoes the concern I raised above.
In France, a
Coface study
published on 17 November 2026 also shows job postings falling behind in the most exposed occupations, including roles for experienced workers. It can’t establish that AI caused the drop.
These studies don’t prove my 80% scenario. They show that the question has moved beyond theory.

sections.title: A society that could become much more unequal

content.text: My biggest concern goes beyond the jobs that might disappear. I worry about the effects on society as a whole.

If automated systems handle a growing share of production, who will benefit from the productivity gains? Employees? Consumers paying lower prices? Or mainly businesses and the owners of those technologies?

I fear wealth will become increasingly concentrated. On one side are people who own businesses, products, infrastructure or capital. On the other is a growing share of the population whose skills are losing value on the job market.
The
International Monetary Fund
has already pointed to this risk: AI could widen wealth inequality by increasing returns on capital. Much depends on how the gains are shared.

I’m also worried about greater social and political polarisation. If some people see their career prospects dim while others get rich quickly, trust in our institutions could take a hit. That could bring more insecurity, tension, resentment and political instability.
None of this is inevitable. Public policy, redistribution, training and social protection will all matter.
There are more optimistic projections. In 2025, the
World Economic Forum
projected a net increase of 78 million jobs worldwide by 2030. The estimate is based on the expectations of employers surveyed and takes account of several major shifts, including AI.
But I’d rather consider the difficult scenario and prepare for it than stake everything on our collective ability to absorb the shock with minimal harm.

sections.title: I don’t want to wait until it affects me

content.text: Faced with a change this big, it’s easy to feel powerless. What can one person do? That’s exactly why I think we should start thinking about it now.
There’s no need to switch careers tomorrow or walk away from years of work. But it’s time to ask a question we’ve rarely needed to take this seriously:
If my skills lost much of their value over the next ten years, what could I rely on to keep living well?

For some people, the answer will be to specialise in a field that’s harder to automate. Others might go independent, build up assets, create a product or develop skills that involve working in the physical world.

There’s probably no universal strategy. Someone who likes starting businesses, taking risks and selling will have different options from someone who values stability, prefers working alone and hates approaching potential customers.
That’s what made me want to build a tool.

sections.title: A tool for thinking through your own strategy

content.text: I wondered if I could help people take a step back from their situation and spot some directions to explore over the coming years. I wanted to help people find options they might not have thought of. Predicting their future or telling them which job to choose was never the aim.

Take two examples. A creative, independent person who wants to start a business but feels uncomfortable selling could explore building a small product that earns recurring revenue, ideally with a partner who enjoys sales.

Someone else who enjoys meeting people and doing practical work could consider moving gradually into a role that combines close contact with customers, technical skills and hands-on work in the field.
Both people are preparing for the same risk, but their paths look very different.
I put together a short interactive journey to explore five directions for thinking about how AI could affect work.
It starts out like a classic questionnaire. I’ll let you discover the rest: it only takes a few minutes.
It isn’t a psychological test or personalised advice. Just a starting point to structure your thinking without starting from a blank page.

sections.title: The goal is not to become irreplaceable

content.text: An idea comes up a lot in conversations about AI: we should develop skills that machines will never be able to replace. I’m not convinced.

For one thing, nobody really knows what these systems will be capable of in ten years. For another, a skill can still be useful while losing much of its value on the job market. Being excellent at your job doesn’t guarantee that a company will still need to pay as many people to do it.
I prefer to look at it differently. What if we tried to become a little less dependent over time on our ability to sell our labour, without devoting all our efforts to becoming irreplaceable?

That could mean owning assets, developing a second source of income, learning to use AI well, building a reputation, keeping up a professional network or developing skills you can use across several sectors.
These are possibilities. A product can fail, an investment can lose value, and a career change can prove difficult. But having several options means you aren’t staking everything on one.

sections.title: In ten years, I’d like to know I planned ahead

content.text: I could be wrong about the scale of what’s happening. Maybe AI will create many more jobs than it destroys. Maybe progress will slow down. Maybe we’ll find a new balance together. I sincerely hope so.

But if my scenario comes close to reality, those who start thinking about it and making more options for themselves today will have valuable room to manoeuvre. I don’t want to wait until it affects me directly to start asking the right questions.
I think we’re going through a major transition, and the next five to ten years could change the way we work, make a living and organise society.
The question I want to ask goes beyond which job to choose:
How can I do things now that give me some freedom later, even if the world of work changes radically?
That’s what I wanted to encourage people to think about, with this article and with the tool.
